title: Why are you a nincompoop? | INSULTS

entries.note: A surprisingly violent word, cognate with [[same-root:assault]]; both go back to Latin [[from:salire]], to leap, so an insult is leaping at someone verbally.
Cognate with [[same-root:insult]], from Latin [[from:salire]], to leap; it means leaping at someone physically.
One of Jess's favourite insult phenomena, pairing words like fart with nugget; [[see:Colin Morris]] charted the commonest ones on Reddit, and the more unexpected, the funnier.
A programmer and Reddit user who in 2022 assembled a grid of the most common [[see:compound insult]]s on Reddit.
An example of a [[see:compound insult]] formed by matching fart with words like muffin, goblin, waffle or nugget.
Given as a good, common, more obvious [[see:compound insult]].
A less expected [[see:compound insult]] you might occasionally run into.
When a word goes from being insulting or pejorative to inoffensive; also discussed on a previous episode; examples include [[see:queer]], [[see:brat]] and [[see:nerd]].
An example of [[see:amelioration]]: once an insult, now reclaimed by the LGBTQ community.
An insult currently undergoing [[see:amelioration]], popularised by [[see:Charli XCX]]'s album; the word of the season, about embracing your perhaps negative qualities.
A twist on [[see:hot girl summer]], more in-your-face, about proudly embracing negative qualities, popularised by [[see:Charli XCX]].
Singer whose album popularised [[see:brat]] and linked it with a shade of green.
The particular shade of green associated with [[see:brat]], designed to be deliberately uneasy on the eye.
The phrase that [[see:brat summer]] twists into something more intrusive and in-your-face.
An old insult for someone taking up unnecessary space on the planet, an [[see:encumbrance]] to others; cumber goes back to Latin [[from:cumulus]].
From the idea of being blocked by a heap, Latin [[from:cumulus]], such as a pile of rocks in the road; the key to [[see:cumberworld]].
Meant a heap, like a pile of rocks blocking a road, giving [[gave:encumbrance]]; a cumulus cloud is a big pile of fluffiness in the sky.
The king of the old-fashioned insult, whose ability to coin them is one of his great gifts; Rob reads several from a mug his dad gave him.

entries.term: I desire we may be better strangers
entries.note: A [[see:William Shakespeare]] insult from Rob's mug, one of his favourites for being so withering.
A [[see:William Shakespeare]] insult read from Rob's mug.
A not terribly nice [[see:William Shakespeare]] insult from Rob's mug.
A [[see:William Shakespeare]] line from Rob's mug that he suspects is more a description than an insult.

entries.term: anointed sovereign of sighs and groans
entries.note: A [[see:William Shakespeare]] insult from Rob's mug, which Jess finds incredible.
Shakespeare character to whom Jess suspects most of the single-phrase insults belong, given his huge insult-filled rants in the history plays.
Opens one of the insult-packed rants in [[see:William Shakespeare]]'s history plays that Jess quotes.
One of the string of insults in a [[see:William Shakespeare]] history-play rant quoted by Jess.

Ends the string of insults in a [[see:William Shakespeare]] history-play rant quoted by Jess.
One of a run of [[see:William Shakespeare]] insults Jess quotes, alongside [[see:rampallion]] and [[see:fustilarian]].
One of a run of [[see:William Shakespeare]] insults Jess quotes, alongside [[see:scullion]] and [[see:fustilarian]].
One of a run of [[see:William Shakespeare]] insults Jess quotes, alongside [[see:scullion]] and [[see:rampallion]].
The threat that caps a run of [[see:William Shakespeare]] insults Jess quotes.
The pre-Shakespearean sport of hurling insults at one another, exemplified early by [[see:The Flyting of Dunbar and Kennedy]].

entries.term: The Flyting of Dunbar and Kennedy
entries.note: One of the earliest examples of [[see:flyting]], published around 1400–1500, detailing a huge insult face-off between a court poet and a parson.
A 13th-century Middle English poem that is essentially a rap battle of insults between an owl and a [[see:nightingale]].
Literally means night singer, fitting the owl's complaint in [[see:The Owl and the Nightingale]] that it sings all the time.
Body-language insults, which Desmond Morris divides into ten categories, from uninterest and boredom to mockery and symbolic signals like hand gestures.
Words for being drunk, the subject of a Rob newsletter; [[see:Michael McIntyre]] joked that English speakers can turn almost any word into one.
Comedian with a bit about how English people can use just about any word to mean drunk, like [[see:gazeboed]] or [[see:car-parked]].
One of the established [[see:drunkonyms]].
One of the established [[see:drunkonyms]].
One of the established [[see:drunkonyms]].
One of the established [[see:drunkonyms]].
A joke drunk word from [[see:Michael McIntyre]], who suggested you could claim to be utterly gazeboed.
A joke drunk word from [[see:Michael McIntyre]], who suggested you could be thoroughly car-parked.
Rob's attempt at a new drunk word fails because mugged already has another meaning.
Rejected as a new drunk word because it already means hit.
Rob's successful invented drunk word, though Jess thinks it could be a euphemism for something else.
Coined by WWI Australian soldiers for artillery shells that [[from:plonk]]ed down, then a penis; softened enough for [[see:Only Fools and Horses]], going through pejoration and amelioration.
To put something down unceremoniously or let it fall, the verb behind Australian soldiers' [[gave:plonker]] for artillery shells.
A phrase for a private male pastime, which made calling someone a [[see:plonker]] the same as calling them a [[see:tosser]].
Equivalent in origin and meaning to calling someone a [[see:plonker]].
1980s–90s primetime British comedy whose catchphrase 'you plonker, Rodney' shows how much [[see:plonker]] had softened.
The stage [[see:plonker]] went through, becoming more aggressive before its [[see:amelioration]].
Once an actual legal designation, now a milder, less serious insult, like [[see:lunatic]].
Like [[see:idiot]], once a clinical or legal term, now used more mildly as an insult.
A perfectly scientific word, in the name of an English society now called Scope, until playground misuse made it unusable.
Its shortening is now much ruder, and after long insulting use it is rarely used clinically, though the word lacks that stigma in other languages.
A standard Victorian word for enfeebled, used by the Romans as an insult; probably from Latin [[from?:baculum]], walking stick, someone lacking support.
First seen in the 13th century meaning gentle or mild, later extended to soft-witted or dull; now a mild, even loving insult.
Schoolyard lore linked it to whale anatomy, but it is probably just a variation of [[from?:dick]].
No longer heated, from Old Norse [[from:kumba]], a block of wood, so a chump is literally a blockhead.
A pejorative, intensifying ending meaning too much, as in [[see:drunkard]], [[see:braggart]], [[see:dullard]], [[see:bastard]], [[see:wizard]] and [[see:mustard]].
Someone who drinks too much, an example of the intensifying [[see:-ard]] ending.
Someone who brags too much, an example of the intensifying [[see:-ard]] ending.
Someone quite dull or very stupid, an example of the intensifying [[see:-ard]] ending.
Literally someone very wise; not an insult but shows the same intensifying [[see:-ard]] ending.
A bird you don't want to see every day, given as another negative word with the [[see:-ard]] ending.
[[from:must]] plus the intensifying [[see:-ard]], implying an intense flavour: extremely musty.
The dregs of winemaking, the seeds and crushed-up stuff, which with [[see:-ard]] gave [[gave:mustard]].
Has the [[see:-ard]] ending but comes from Latin [[from:cauda]], tail, as in [[see:coda]], someone who tucks tail and runs; unrelated to [[unrelated:cower]] despite folk-etymological conflation.
Apparently unrelated to [[unrelated:coward]], though folk etymology conflated the two and Rob thinks the association fits better.
From an Old French word meaning pack-saddle son, [[from:fils de bast]], a child conceived on the road; also Rob's default caption text.
A child conceived while travelling, the saddle doubling as a bed, perhaps with someone other than one's spouse; source of [[gave:bastard]].
The most famous [[see:bastard]], [[see:William the Conqueror]], was known by this name first; it's unclear whether friends or enemies gave it.
Had a huge impact on English; before this name he was known as [[see:Guillaume le Bâtard]].
Originally a type of pie, so the pastry was part of the dish and a [[see:custard tart]] should really just be called a custard.
Rob argues it should simply be called a [[see:custard]], since the pastry was part of the original dish.
A popular English snack that, like a [[see:custard tart]], is really just what a [[see:custard]] originally was.
An insult perhaps from [[see:custard]]'s yellowness, but really from the way it wobbles when it sets; compare [[equivalent:quaking custard]].
An old insult, sadly no longer used, from how [[see:custard]] wobbles; like [[equivalent:cowardy custard]].
From the biblical hunter Nimrod; used ironically of [[see:Elmer Fudd]] in Looney Tunes, after [[see:Nimrod Wildfire]], becoming a 1960s American insult.
Looney Tunes character called a [[see:nimrod]], ironically comparing him to a great hunter.
A caricature of [[see:Davy Crockett]] in several mid-1800s plays, linking [[see:nimrod]] with cartoonish hunters before Elmer Fudd.
Caricatured as [[see:Nimrod Wildfire]] in mid-1800s plays.
Origin uncertain: perhaps from [[from?:Nicodemus]], or from [[from?:non compos mentis]] influenced by [[see:ninny]]; also spelled nickumpoop, recalling [[see:Nick]].
The Pharisee whose role in the Bible is asking Jesus stupid questions, in the biblical theory for [[see:nincompoop]].
A Latin phrase about soundness of mind still sometimes used today; a possible source of [[gave?:nincompoop]].
A fool, short for [[from:innocent]], meaning naively stupid; possibly an influence on [[see:nincompoop]].
Previously discussed as a recurring reference to the devil, recalled by the spelling nickumpoop for [[see:nincompoop]].
An insult found in a [[see:nincompoop]] citation ('pitiful lousy Tom Farthing'); it sounds Dickensian or like a [[see:Jack Sprat]]-type character.
The kind of character [[see:Tom Farthing]] sounds like.
An obsequious flatterer, from Greek for fig: one who shows the fig ([[from:showing the fig]]), maybe as politicians' supporters taunting opponents.
A rude Greek hand gesture probably implying female genitalia, possibly linked to servile followers, giving [[gave:sycophant]].
A thoroughly ameliorated insult about a century old, once spelled nert, probably a college slang variant of [[from?:nut]]; also appears in [[see:If I Ran the Zoo]].
Dr Seuss book using [[see:nerd]] as an imaginary creature's name, not thought to have much influenced the insult.
Probably from Dutch for fool or Scandinavian to mock; a sideshow performer biting off live animals' heads, popularised by [[see:Nightmare Alley]], later computer enthusiasts.
1940s film, recently remade, that popularised the sideshow sense of [[see:geek]].
A more insulting way of saying someone is very into something, as in [[see:Jesus freak]]; still fairly pejorative though partly ameliorated, as in [[see:book freak]].
An example of the pejorative [[see:freak]] for someone very into something.
Something people might proudly call themselves, showing amelioration of [[see:freak]].
Originally meant being into things outside the ordinary in the bedroom, a consensually naughty sense of [[see:freak]].
1500s English writer and critic whose The Art of English Poesy dissected rhetoric of disdain, sarcasm and mockery, like [[see:mycterismus]] and [[see:asteismus]].
Literally a turning up of the nose, a form of mockery described by [[see:George Puttenham]], who also called it the [[equivalent:fleering frump]].
[[see:George Puttenham]]'s English name for [[equivalent:mycterismus]].
Expressing a disagreeable thing agreeably, almost a backhanded compliment, in [[see:George Puttenham]]'s scheme; also called the [[equivalent:privy nip]].
[[see:George Puttenham]]'s English name for [[equivalent:charientismus]], a mock given under smooth and lowly words.
Literally sarcasm, in [[see:George Puttenham]]'s scheme, also called the [[equivalent:bitter taunt]].
[[see:George Puttenham]]'s English name for [[equivalent:sarcasmus]].
In [[see:George Puttenham]]'s scheme, also called the [[equivalent:merry scoff]] or the [[equivalent:civil jest]].
One of [[see:George Puttenham]]'s English names for [[equivalent:asteismus]].
One of [[see:George Puttenham]]'s English names for [[equivalent:asteismus]].
